newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian industry gas rate cut impact seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Russian industry gas rate cut impact seen limited.

text.p: Russia's decision to lower natural gas tariffs by up to 40 percent for debt-plagued domestic enterprises may not be the boon to big energy users it appears, energy analysts said on Friday.

President Boris Yeltsin signed a decree "On Lowering Gas Prices for Russian Users" on Thursday. But details of the decree showed reductions would only apply to firms which had fully paid off their debts no later than December 31, 1997.
The presidential press service did not clarify which debts should be paid off, but Gazprom said on Friday the decree was referring to debts owed by domestic industries to the monopoly.

"For those consumers which liquidate their arrears to Gazprom and carry out payments (on time), RAO Gazprom will create a reduction (in gas tariffs)" Lira Rosenova, advisor to company chairman Rem Vyakhirev, said.
The presidential service also said consumers had to pay in cash, in advance, for supplies.
The tariff cut is part of a wider drive by Moscow's reformist economic heavyweights to reign in burgeoning debts which plague the giant energy sector.
The government has proposed share and bond issues, asset transfers and even bankruptcy to help force indebted Soviet-era oil, gas and electricity monoliths to cough up their tax and other debts.
Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas company, complains its customers cannot pay for supplies, in turn causing Gazprom to fall behind on payments to the government.
Gazprom welcomed the move to cut gas tariffs, saying it would help chip away at the mountainous arrears owed to it by the industrial sector.

"It is helpful for the consumers, because they receive gas at cheaper rates, helpful for us because we get money, and it is good for the budget because we pay taxes on what we receive," Rosenova said.
But analysts said the payment condition could dilute the impact of the tariff cuts significantly.
"Even with this incentive, a lot of big companies will not have the cash to pay off their debts by year-end," said Dan Lubash, managing director of Emerging Markets Europe at Merrill Lynch in London.

Stephen O'Sullivan, director of oil and gas at MC Securities Ltd in London, said the rate reduction was part of wider reform of Russia's archaic energy price system, whereby industrial users have been subsidising domestic consumers for many years.
"In the past the industry has subsidised domestic users," he said, adding domestic gas users were likely to face higher gas costs in future while industry price continued to fall.

Creditanstalt Investment Bank Russia estimated Russian companies owed Gazprom a massive 58 trillion roubles ($10.2 billion). It also said Gazprom receives payments for only 40 percent of all domestic sales.

Fuel and Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov has been charged with injecting more competition to Russia's so-called "natural monopolies", including the gas and power industries, where competition is almost non-existent.
He is also cracking down on tax and payment debtors in an attempt to bring federal budget income into line with spending.

First Deputy Fuel and Energy Minister Sergei Kiriyenko said on Tuesday that electricity stations belonging to national power giant Unified Energy System (UES) could be handed over to Gazprom to help pay of intercompany debts.
He said UES stations alone owed Gazprom around 35 trillion roubles ($6.1 billion). The power industry is a major industrial gas consumer.

Gazprom, with a third of the world's gas reserves, produced 565 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas in 1996, up 5.2 bcm on 1995 levels. It accounts for around 95 percent of Russian gas output. Its non-CIS exports in 1996 were 123.5 bcm, up 6.1 bcm from 1995.
